claim: PTPδ, PTPσ, and LAR are the three LAR-RPTPs expressed in the brain.
source: Three LAR-RPTPs – PTPδ, PTPσ, and LAR – are expressed in the brain, bind to the active zone scaffolding protein Liprin-α and to synaptic cell-adhesion proteins, and recruit presynaptic material in artificial synapse formation assays (Bomkamp et al., 2019; Han et al., 2018; Han et al., 2020a; Johnson and Van Vactor, 2003; Kwon et al., 2010; Pulido et al., 1995; Serra-Pagès et al., 1998; Takahashi et al., 2011; Yim et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature establishing LAR-RPTP expression in brain.

claim: LAR-RPTPs bind to the active zone scaffolding protein Liprin-α.
source: Three LAR-RPTPs – PTPδ, PTPσ, and LAR – are expressed in the brain, bind to the active zone scaffolding protein Liprin-α and to synaptic cell-adhesion proteins, and recruit presynaptic material in artificial synapse formation assays (Bomkamp et al., 2019; Han et al., 2018; Han et al., 2020a; Johnson and Van Vactor, 2003; Kwon et al., 2010; Pulido et al., 1995; Serra-Pagès et al., 1998; Takahashi et al., 2011; Yim et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies demonstrating binding interactions.

claim: LAR-RPTPs bind to synaptic cell-adhesion proteins.
source: Three LAR-RPTPs – PTPδ, PTPσ, and LAR – are expressed in the brain, bind to the active zone scaffolding protein Liprin-α and to synaptic cell-adhesion proteins, and recruit presynaptic material in artificial synapse formation assays (Bomkamp et al., 2019; Han et al., 2018; Han et al., 2020a; Johnson and Van Vactor, 2003; Kwon et al., 2010; Pulido et al., 1995; Serra-Pagès et al., 1998; Takahashi et al., 2011; Yim et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: LAR-RPTPs recruit presynaptic material in artificial synapse formation assays.
source: Three LAR-RPTPs – PTPδ, PTPσ, and LAR – are expressed in the brain, bind to the active zone scaffolding protein Liprin-α and to synaptic cell-adhesion proteins, and recruit presynaptic material in artificial synapse formation assays (Bomkamp et al., 2019; Han et al., 2018; Han et al., 2020a; Johnson and Van Vactor, 2003; Kwon et al., 2010; Pulido et al., 1995; Serra-Pagès et al., 1998; Takahashi et al., 2011; Yim et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in LAR-RPTPs in invertebrates resulted in defects in axon guidance.
source: In invertebrates, loss-of-function mutations in LAR-RPTPs resulted in defects in axon guidance, increased active zone and synapse areas, and impaired neurotransmitter secretion (Ackley et al., 2005; Clandinin et al., 2001; Desai et al., 1997; Kaufmann et al., 2002; Krueger et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior invertebrate studies.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in LAR-RPTPs in invertebrates resulted in increased active zone and synapse areas.
source: In invertebrates, loss-of-function mutations in LAR-RPTPs resulted in defects in axon guidance, increased active zone and synapse areas, and impaired neurotransmitter secretion (Ackley et al., 2005; Clandinin et al., 2001; Desai et al., 1997; Kaufmann et al., 2002; Krueger et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior invertebrate studies.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in LAR-RPTPs in invertebrates resulted in impaired neurotransmitter secretion.
source: In invertebrates, loss-of-function mutations in LAR-RPTPs resulted in defects in axon guidance, increased active zone and synapse areas, and impaired neurotransmitter secretion (Ackley et al., 2005; Clandinin et al., 2001; Desai et al., 1997; Kaufmann et al., 2002; Krueger et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior invertebrate studies.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of LAR-RPTPs in mice caused generalized loss of synapse markers.
source: In mice, RNAi-mediated knockdown of LAR-RPTPs or deletion of PTPσ caused generalized loss of synapse markers and defective synaptic transmission (Dunah et al., 2005; Han et al., 2018; Han et al., 2020a; Han et al., 2020b), leading to the model that LAR-RPTPs control synapse formation.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior RNAi studies in mice.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of LAR-RPTPs in mice caused defective synaptic transmission.
source: In mice, RNAi-mediated knockdown of LAR-RPTPs or deletion of PTPσ caused generalized loss of synapse markers and defective synaptic transmission (Dunah et al., 2005; Han et al., 2018; Han et al., 2020a; Han et al., 2020b), leading to the model that LAR-RPTPs control synapse formation.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior RNAi studies in mice.

claim: Deletion of PTPσ in mice caused generalized loss of synapse markers.
source: In mice, RNAi-mediated knockdown of LAR-RPTPs or deletion of PTPσ caused generalized loss of synapse markers and defective synaptic transmission (Dunah et al., 2005; Han et al., 2018; Han et al., 2020a; Han et al., 2020b), leading to the model that LAR-RPTPs control synapse formation.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior genetic studies in mice.

claim: Deletion of PTPσ in mice caused defective synaptic transmission.
source: In mice, RNAi-mediated knockdown of LAR-RPTPs or deletion of PTPσ caused generalized loss of synapse markers and defective synaptic transmission (Dunah et al., 2005; Han et al., 2018; Han et al., 2020a; Han et al., 2020b), leading to the model that LAR-RPTPs control synapse formation.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior genetic studies in mice.

claim: Mild synaptic and behavioral defects were observed in single gene constitutive knockouts of LAR-RPTPs.
source: Furthermore, mild synaptic and behavioral defects were observed in single gene constitutive knockouts (Elchebly et al., 1999; Horn et al., 2012; Park et al., 2020; Uetani et al., 2000; Wallace et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior single knockout studies.

claim: A recent study using conditional mouse gene targeting to ablate PTPδ, PTPσ, and LAR found no overt defects in neurotransmitter release.
source: Contrasting the RNAi-based analyses, however, a recent study used conditional mouse gene targeting to ablate PTPδ, PTPσ, and LAR, and found no overt defects in neurotransmitter release (Sclip and Südhof, 2020), thereby questioning the general role of LAR-RPTPs in synapse assembly.
evidence: Supported by citation to a recent independent study.

claim: PTPδ localizes to the synaptic cleft precisely apposed to postsynaptic scaffolds of excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
source: Here, superresolution microscopy reveals that PTPδ localizes to the synaptic cleft precisely apposed to postsynaptic scaffolds of excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
evidence: Supported by STED microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PTPδ is concentrated apposed to PSD-95 at excitatory synapses at distances of 24 ± 17 nm.
source: PTPδ, detected with antibodies against the extracellular fibronectin domains (Shishikura et al., 2016), was concentrated apposed to PSD-95 and Gephyrin, respectively, at distances of 24 ± 17 nm (PSD-95) and 28 ± 11 nm (Gephyrin) (Figure 1D–I).
evidence: Supported by STED microscopy measurements shown in Figure 1D-I.

claim: PTPδ is concentrated apposed to Gephyrin at inhibitory synapses at distances of 28 ± 11 nm.
source: PTPδ, detected with antibodies against the extracellular fibronectin domains (Shishikura et al., 2016), was concentrated apposed to PSD-95 and Gephyrin, respectively, at distances of 24 ± 17 nm (PSD-95) and 28 ± 11 nm (Gephyrin) (Figure 1D–I).
evidence: Supported by STED microscopy measurements shown in Figure 1D-I.

claim: 88% of excitatory synapses contain PTPδ.
source: Furthermore, most synapses contain PTPδ, as 88% of excitatory and 92% of inhibitory synapses had PTPδ peak intensities higher than three standard deviations above the average of the cTKORPTP signal.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of STED microscopy data.

claim: 92% of inhibitory synapses contain PTPδ.
source: Furthermore, most synapses contain PTPδ, as 88% of excitatory and 92% of inhibitory synapses had PTPδ peak intensities higher than three standard deviations above the average of the cTKORPTP signal.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of STED microscopy data.

claim: Synapse density is unchanged in cTKORPTP neurons.
source: However, the synapse density, measured as Synaptophysin puncta, was unchanged in cTKORPTP neurons (Figure 1L–O).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy quantification shown in Figure 1L-O.

claim: Small increases in Synaptophysin puncta intensity were detected in cTKORPTP neurons.
source: Small increases in puncta intensity and area were detected (Figure 1L–O), consistent with enlargements observed in invertebrates (Ackley et al., 2005; Kaufmann et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy quantification shown in Figure 1L-O.

claim: Small increases in Synaptophysin puncta area were detected in cTKORPTP neurons.
source: Small increases in puncta intensity and area were detected (Figure 1L–O), consistent with enlargements observed in invertebrates (Ackley et al., 2005; Kaufmann et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy quantification shown in Figure 1L-O.

claim: A ~15% increase in the total synaptic vesicle number per synapse profile was detected in cTKORPTP neurons.
source: A ~15% increase in the total synaptic vesicle number per synapse profile was detected, matching the modestly increased Synaptophysin signals (Figure 1) and the enhanced presence of vesicular markers in C. elegans mutants (Ackley et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy quantification.

claim: No differences in vesicle docking were observed in cTKORPTP neurons.
source: Notably, no differences in vesicle docking (defined as vesicles for which the electron dense membrane merges with the density of the target membrane) were observed.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy analysis.

claim: Synapse width was increased by ~30% in cTKORPTP neurons.
source: Synapse width, measured as the distance over which the pre- and postsynapse are apposed to one another and separated by a synaptic cleft, was increased by ~30%, again matching invertebrate phenotypes (Kaufmann et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy measurements.

claim: RIM, Munc13-1, CaV2.1, and Liprin-α3 are localized within 30–60 nm of the postsynaptic scaffolds in controlRPTP and cTKORPTP synapses.
source: RIM, Munc13-1, CaV2.1, and Liprin-α3 were localized within 30–60 nm of the postsynaptic scaffolds in controlRPTP and cTKORPTP synapses, as expected for these proteins (Held et al., 2020; Wong et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by STED microscopy measurements and citations to prior studies.

claim: Small increases in RIM were detected in both types of cTKORPTP synapses.
source: Overall, there were no strong changes in their levels, but small increases in RIM and small decreases in Liprin-α3 were detected in both types of cTKORPTP synapses either by STED (Figure 2F–M) or confocal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) microscopy.
evidence: Supported by STED and confocal microscopy quantification shown in Figure 2.

claim: Small decreases in Liprin-α3 were detected in both types of cTKORPTP synapses.
source: Overall, there were no strong changes in their levels, but small increases in RIM and small decreases in Liprin-α3 were detected in both types of cTKORPTP synapses either by STED (Figure 2F–M) or confocal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) microscopy.
evidence: Supported by STED and confocal microscopy quantification shown in Figure 2.

claim: Release evoked by single action potentials was similar between controlRPTP and cTKORPTP neurons.
source: Release evoked by single action potentials was similar between controlRPTP and cTKORPTP neurons, and IPSC kinetics were unaffected.
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology data.

claim: IPSC kinetics were unaffected in cTKORPTP neurons.
source: Release evoked by single action potentials was similar between controlRPTP and cTKORPTP neurons, and IPSC kinetics were unaffected.
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology data.

claim: The IPSC paired pulse ratio was unaffected in cTKORPTP neurons.
source: The IPSC ratio of two consecutive stimuli (paired pulse ratio), which is inversely proportional to vesicular release probability (Zucker and Regehr, 2002), was also unaffected.
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology data and citation to prior literature on paired pulse ratio.

claim: Ablation of LAR-RPTPs from hippocampal neurons does not alter synapse density.
source: Overall, we demonstrate that ablation of LAR-RPTPs from hippocampal neurons does not alter synapse density, synaptic vesicle docking, membrane anchoring of active zones, and synaptic vesicle release.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental approaches including microscopy and electrophysiology.

claim: Ablation of LAR-RPTPs from hippocampal neurons does not alter synaptic vesicle docking.
source: Overall, we demonstrate that ablation of LAR-RPTPs from hippocampal neurons does not alter synapse density, synaptic vesicle docking, membrane anchoring of active zones, and synaptic vesicle release.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data.

claim: Ablation of LAR-RPTPs from hippocampal neurons does not alter membrane anchoring of active zones.
source: Overall, we demonstrate that ablation of LAR-RPTPs from hippocampal neurons does not alter synapse density, synaptic vesicle docking, membrane anchoring of active zones, and synaptic vesicle release.
evidence: Supported by STED microscopy showing normal localization of active zone proteins.

claim: Ablation of LAR-RPTPs from hippocampal neurons does not alter synaptic vesicle release.
source: Overall, we demonstrate that ablation of LAR-RPTPs from hippocampal neurons does not alter synapse density, synaptic vesicle docking, membrane anchoring of active zones, and synaptic vesicle release.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: A parallel study reported no loss of synaptic puncta upon LAR-RPTP knockout in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: This aligns with a parallel study that reported no loss of synaptic puncta and efficient release at excitatory synapses in cultured hippocampal neurons and in acute hippocampal brain slices (Sclip and Südhof, 2020) upon LAR-RPTP knockout, but contrasts RNAi-based studies that led to models in which these RPTPs are major synapse organizers (Dunah et al., 2005; Fukai and Yoshida, 2020; Han et al., 2018; Han et al., 2020a; Han et al., 2020b; Kwon et al., 2010; Takahashi and Craig, 2013; Um and Ko, 2013; Yim et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to a recent independent study.

claim: A parallel study reported efficient release at excitatory synapses upon LAR-RPTP knockout in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: This aligns with a parallel study that reported no loss of synaptic puncta and efficient release at excitatory synapses in cultured hippocampal neurons and in acute hippocampal brain slices (Sclip and Südhof, 2020) upon LAR-RPTP knockout, but contrasts RNAi-based studies that led to models in which these RPTPs are major synapse organizers (Dunah et al., 2005; Fukai and Yoshida, 2020; Han et al., 2018; Han et al., 2020a; Han et al., 2020b; Kwon et al., 2010; Takahashi and Craig, 2013; Um and Ko, 2013; Yim et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to a recent independent study.

claim: A parallel study reported efficient release at excitatory synapses upon LAR-RPTP knockout in acute hippocampal brain slices.
source: This aligns with a parallel study that reported no loss of synaptic puncta and efficient release at excitatory synapses in cultured hippocampal neurons and in acute hippocampal brain slices (Sclip and Südhof, 2020) upon LAR-RPTP knockout, but contrasts RNAi-based studies that led to models in which these RPTPs are major synapse organizers (Dunah et al., 2005; Fukai and Yoshida, 2020; Han et al., 2018; Han et al., 2020a; Han et al., 2020b; Kwon et al., 2010; Takahashi and Craig, 2013; Um and Ko, 2013; Yim et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to a recent independent study.

claim: PTPδ extracellular domains are correctly positioned to locally execute synaptic functions.
source: Our study establishes specific localization of PTPδ extracellular domains to the synaptic cleft. Hence, PTPδ is correctly positioned to locally execute synaptic functions, for example for shaping cleft geometry, to modulate presynaptic plasticity, or to control postsynaptic receptors (Biederer et al., 2017; Sclip and Südhof, 2020; Uetani et al., 2000).
evidence: Inferred from the STED microscopy data showing PTPδ localization at the synaptic cleft.

claim: PTPδ could function in shaping cleft geometry.
source: Our study establishes specific localization of PTPδ extracellular domains to the synaptic cleft. Hence, PTPδ is correctly positioned to locally execute synaptic functions, for example for shaping cleft geometry, to modulate presynaptic plasticity, or to control postsynaptic receptors (Biederer et al., 2017; Sclip and Südhof, 2020; Uetani et al., 2000).
evidence: Speculative based on localization data and citations to prior literature.

claim: PTPδ could function to modulate presynaptic plasticity.
source: Our study establishes specific localization of PTPδ extracellular domains to the synaptic cleft. Hence, PTPδ is correctly positioned to locally execute synaptic functions, for example for shaping cleft geometry, to modulate presynaptic plasticity, or to control postsynaptic receptors (Biederer et al., 2017; Sclip and Südhof, 2020; Uetani et al., 2000).
evidence: Speculative based on localization data and citations to prior literature.

claim: PTPδ could function to control postsynaptic receptors.
source: Our study establishes specific localization of PTPδ extracellular domains to the synaptic cleft. Hence, PTPδ is correctly positioned to locally execute synaptic functions, for example for shaping cleft geometry, to modulate presynaptic plasticity, or to control postsynaptic receptors (Biederer et al., 2017; Sclip and Südhof, 2020; Uetani et al., 2000).
evidence: Speculative based on localization data and citations to prior literature.

claim: Deletion of CaV2 channels produces no major structural defects at synapses.
source: Deletion of the major candidates, CaV2 channels (Held et al., 2020), Neurexins (Chen et al., 2017), and now LAR-PTPs (Figures 1 and 2), produces no major structural defects, indicating that active zones are most likely anchored to the plasma membrane through multiple parallel pathways that may or may not include these proteins (Emperador-Melero and Kaeser, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Deletion of Neurexins produces no major structural defects at synapses.
source: Deletion of the major candidates, CaV2 channels (Held et al., 2020), Neurexins (Chen et al., 2017), and now LAR-PTPs (Figures 1 and 2), produces no major structural defects, indicating that active zones are most likely anchored to the plasma membrane through multiple parallel pathways that may or may not include these proteins (Emperador-Melero and Kaeser, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Active zones are most likely anchored to the plasma membrane through multiple parallel pathways.
source: Deletion of the major candidates, CaV2 channels (Held et al., 2020), Neurexins (Chen et al., 2017), and now LAR-PTPs (Figures 1 and 2), produces no major structural defects, indicating that active zones are most likely anchored to the plasma membrane through multiple parallel pathways that may or may not include these proteins (Emperador-Melero and Kaeser, 2020).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of major defects after deletion of multiple candidate proteins and supported by citation.

claim: The PTPδ allele contains loxP sites flanking exon 23.
source: PTPδ and PTPσ alleles contain loxP sites flanking exons 23 and 4, respectively.
evidence: Supported by the gene targeting strategy diagram in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The PTPσ allele contains loxP sites flanking exon 4.
source: PTPδ and PTPσ alleles contain loxP sites flanking exons 23 and 4, respectively.
evidence: Supported by the gene targeting strategy diagram in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The LAR allele contains loxP sites flanking exons 8, 9, and 10.
source: The LAR allele contains loxp sites flanking exons 8, 9, and 10 and was obtained at the embryonic stem cell stage from the Helmholtz Zentrum München (Ptprftm1a(EUCOMM)Wtsi).
evidence: Supported by the gene targeting strategy diagram in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The floxed alleles for each LAR-RPTP gene did not impair survival.
source: The floxed alleles for each gene did not impair survival and RPTP protein expression was readily detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: RPTP protein expression was readily detected in mice with floxed alleles.
source: The floxed alleles for each gene did not impair survival and RPTP protein expression was readily detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cre recombinase delivered at DIV6 by lentiviruses resulted in removal of PTPδ, PTPσ, and LAR.
source: In cultured hippocampal neurons, Cre recombinase was delivered at DIV6 by lentiviruses and expressed from a Synapsin promotor (Liu et al., 2014) and resulted in removal of PTPδ, PTPσ, and LAR, generating cTKORPTP neurons (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Most PTPδ is likely presynaptic and localized at the active zone.
source: Given the presynaptic roles of LAR-RPTPs at invertebrate synapses and in synapse formation assays (Ackley et al., 2005; Kaufmann et al., 2002), the interactions with the active zone protein Liprin-α (Pulido et al., 1995; Serra-Pagès et al., 1998; Wong et al., 2018), and the asymmetry of the average STED side-view profile of PTPδ with a bias toward the presynapse (Figure 1F,I), it is likely that most PTPδ is presynaptic and localized at the active zone, but postsynaptic components cannot be excluded.
evidence: Inferred from STED data showing asymmetry toward presynapse and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Postsynaptic components of PTPδ cannot be excluded.
source: Given the presynaptic roles of LAR-RPTPs at invertebrate synapses and in synapse formation assays (Ackley et al., 2005; Kaufmann et al., 2002), the interactions with the active zone protein Liprin-α (Pulido et al., 1995; Serra-Pagès et al., 1998; Wong et al., 2018), and the asymmetry of the average STED side-view profile of PTPδ with a bias toward the presynapse (Figure 1F,I), it is likely that most PTPδ is presynaptic and localized at the active zone, but postsynaptic components cannot be excluded.
evidence: Acknowledged limitation based on the resolution and nature of the localization data.

claim: LAR-RPTPs may control assembly of a specific subset of synapses.
source: It remains possible that LAR-RPTPs control assembly of a specific subset of synapses, which may explain why PTPδ ablation causes modest layer-specific impairments of synaptic strength (Park et al., 2020).
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citation to prior study showing layer-specific effects.

claim: LAR-RPTPs may shape aspects of the synaptic cleft.
source: LAR-RPTPs may shape aspects of the synaptic cleft, consistent with their localization and transsynaptic interactions and possibly similar to other synaptic cell-adhesion proteins, for example SynCAMs (Perez de Arce et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on localization data and citation to prior study of similar proteins.

claim: The higher levels of RIM may be compensatory to reductions in Liprin-α3.
source: The higher levels of RIM may be compensatory to reductions in Liprin-α3 and could be related to the liquid–liquid phase separation properties of both proteins (Emperador-Melero et al., 2020; McDonald et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the data supported by citations to prior studies on phase separation.

claim: Binding between Liprin-α and LAR-RPTPs may explain Liprin-α3 reductions.
source: While binding between Liprin-α and LAR-RPTPs (Pulido et al., 1995; Serra-Pagès et al., 1998) may explain Liprin-α3 reductions, these data establish that other pathways are sufficient to recruit most Liprin-α3 to active zones.
evidence: Inferred from the data and supported by citations to prior studies showing binding interactions.

claim: Other pathways are sufficient to recruit most Liprin-α3 to active zones.
source: While binding between Liprin-α and LAR-RPTPs (Pulido et al., 1995; Serra-Pagès et al., 1998) may explain Liprin-α3 reductions, these data establish that other pathways are sufficient to recruit most Liprin-α3 to active zones.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Liprin-α3 is still present at active zones despite LAR-RPTP knockout.

claim: The active zone remains assembled in the absence of LAR-RPTPs.
source: Overall, we conclude that the active zone remains assembled and anchored to the target membrane in the absence of LAR-RPTPs.
evidence: Supported by STED microscopy data showing normal localization of active zone proteins.

claim: The active zone remains anchored to the target membrane in the absence of LAR-RPTPs.
source: Overall, we conclude that the active zone remains assembled and anchored to the target membrane in the absence of LAR-RPTPs.
evidence: Supported by STED microscopy data showing normal localization of active zone proteins.

claim: A previous study found that LAR-RPTP ablation induced no strong defects in glutamate release.
source: A previous study found that LAR-RPTP ablation induced no strong defects in glutamate release, but regulated NMDARs through a transsynaptic mechanism (Sclip and Südhof, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: A previous study found that LAR-RPTP ablation regulated NMDARs through a transsynaptic mechanism.
source: A previous study found that LAR-RPTP ablation induced no strong defects in glutamate release, but regulated NMDARs through a transsynaptic mechanism (Sclip and Südhof, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Synaptic vesicle exocytosis monitored via IPSCs is not impaired by LAR-RPTP knockout.
source: We conclude that synaptic vesicle exocytosis, here monitored via IPSCs, is not impaired by LAR-RPTP knockout.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data showing normal IPSCs.

claim: Synapses persist upon LAR-RPTP ablation.
source: Altogether, we conclude that, while biochemical and synapse formation assays support synaptogenic activities for these proteins, synapses persist upon LAR-RPTP ablation, and their structure and function do not necessitate these proteins.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental approaches showing normal synapse density and structure.

claim: Synapse structure does not necessitate LAR-RPTPs.
source: Altogether, we conclude that, while biochemical and synapse formation assays support synaptogenic activities for these proteins, synapses persist upon LAR-RPTP ablation, and their structure and function do not necessitate these proteins.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy and STED microscopy data.

claim: Synapse function does not necessitate LAR-RPTPs.
source: Altogether, we conclude that, while biochemical and synapse formation assays support synaptogenic activities for these proteins, synapses persist upon LAR-RPTP ablation, and their structure and function do not necessitate these proteins.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data showing normal synaptic transmission.

claim: LAR-RPTPs are dispensable for presynapse structure.
source: Hence, despite their localization at synaptic appositions, LAR-RPTPs are dispensable for presynapse structure and function.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy and STED microscopy data showing normal presynaptic structure.

claim: LAR-RPTPs are dispensable for presynapse function.
source: Hence, despite their localization at synaptic appositions, LAR-RPTPs are dispensable for presynapse structure and function.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data showing normal synaptic transmission.

claim: Mild effects on synaptic vesicle clustering were detected after LAR-RPTP ablation.
source: While mild effects on synaptic vesicle clustering and active zone architecture were detected, synapse numbers and their overall structure were unaffected, membrane anchoring of the active zone persisted, and vesicle docking and release were normal.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data showing increased vesicle numbers.

claim: Mild effects on active zone architecture were detected after LAR-RPTP ablation.
source: While mild effects on synaptic vesicle clustering and active zone architecture were detected, synapse numbers and their overall structure were unaffected, membrane anchoring of the active zone persisted, and vesicle docking and release were normal.
evidence: Supported by STED microscopy data showing small changes in RIM and Liprin-α3.

claim: Synapse numbers were unaffected after LAR-RPTP ablation.
source: While mild effects on synaptic vesicle clustering and active zone architecture were detected, synapse numbers and their overall structure were unaffected, membrane anchoring of the active zone persisted, and vesicle docking and release were normal.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data showing normal synapse density.

claim: Overall synapse structure was unaffected after LAR-RPTP ablation.
source: While mild effects on synaptic vesicle clustering and active zone architecture were detected, synapse numbers and their overall structure were unaffected, membrane anchoring of the active zone persisted, and vesicle docking and release were normal.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data.

claim: Membrane anchoring of the active zone persisted after LAR-RPTP ablation.
source: While mild effects on synaptic vesicle clustering and active zone architecture were detected, synapse numbers and their overall structure were unaffected, membrane anchoring of the active zone persisted, and vesicle docking and release were normal.
evidence: Supported by STED microscopy data showing normal localization of active zone proteins.

claim: Vesicle docking was normal after LAR-RPTP ablation.
source: While mild effects on synaptic vesicle clustering and active zone architecture were detected, synapse numbers and their overall structure were unaffected, membrane anchoring of the active zone persisted, and vesicle docking and release were normal.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data.

claim: Vesicle release was normal after LAR-RPTP ablation.
source: While mild effects on synaptic vesicle clustering and active zone architecture were detected, synapse numbers and their overall structure were unaffected, membrane anchoring of the active zone persisted, and vesicle docking and release were normal.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: The PTPδ allele is identical to previously reported alleles.
source: Alleles for PTPδ (Farhy-Tselnicker et al., 2017; Sclip and Südhof, 2020) and PTPσ (Bunin et al., 2015; Sclip and Südhof, 2020) were identical to previously reported alleles, while the LAR allele was newly generated.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies using the same allele.

claim: The PTPσ allele is identical to previously reported alleles.
source: Alleles for PTPδ (Farhy-Tselnicker et al., 2017; Sclip and Südhof, 2020) and PTPσ (Bunin et al., 2015; Sclip and Südhof, 2020) were identical to previously reported alleles, while the LAR allele was newly generated.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies using the same allele.

claim: The LAR allele was newly generated.
source: Alleles for PTPδ (Farhy-Tselnicker et al., 2017; Sclip and Südhof, 2020) and PTPσ (Bunin et al., 2015; Sclip and Südhof, 2020) were identical to previously reported alleles, while the LAR allele was newly generated.
evidence: Stated directly in the manuscript.

claim: LAR-RPTP ablation does not strongly impair synapse ultrastructure.
source: These data establish that LAR-RPTP ablation does not strongly impair synapse ultrastructure.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data showing mostly normal ultrastructure.

claim: The time course of deletion in knockout experiments is similar to the time course used in most RNAi-knockdown studies.
source: We note, however, that the time course of deletion in our knockout experiments is similar to the time course that is used in most RNAi-knockdown studies, and is hence unlikely to explain the differences.
evidence: Based on knowledge of experimental timelines in the field.

claim: Off-target effects of knockdowns may generate artifacts in synapse formation experiments.
source: Other contributing factors could be different experimental preparations and off-target effects of knockdowns, which may generate artifacts in synapse formation experiments (Südhof, 2018).

claim: LAR-RPTPs have upstream functions in neurite outgrowth.
source: Such functions would not be at odds with the at most mild structural and functional effects after LAR-RPTP ablation, nor with upstream functions in neurite outgrowth and axon targeting (Ackley et al., 2005; Clandinin et al., 2001; Desai et al., 1997; Krueger et al., 1996; Prakash et al., 2009; Shishikura et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Synaptic cell-adhesion proteins including SynCAMs, EphBs, Cadherins, Teneurins, and FLRTs are plausible candidates that could contribute to active zone membrane anchoring.
source: Synaptic cell-adhesion proteins that contribute to synapse formation and function, for example SynCAMs, EphBs, Cadherins, Teneurins, and FLRTs, are plausible candidates that could act on their own or in concert with other proteins, including LAR-RPTPs, to contribute to active zone membrane anchoring (Biederer et al., 2017; Südhof, 2018).
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior reviews.
